events.title: A leg set under the warm water
events.body: At Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh the keeper of the basins sets a leg broken through the skin under the warm water of the third basin, binds it tight with wet bark and cord, and turns the man twice a day for a season; he walks out on a stick before the winter turns.

events.title: The keeper of the basins judges a wound by its smell
events.body: The keeper of the warm basins tells by the colour of a wound, and its smell when the dressing comes off, whether it wants the second basin or the third or neither, and has no words for the telling.

events.title: The youth of the south-east asks to go down
events.body: A youth not yet grown to his height asks to be the one let down into the eastern shaft at Toll-dubh, and two women of the south-east plait a rope for it from the hides of three oxen.

events.title: The lamp goes small in the eastern shaft
events.body: The youth is let down into the eastern shaft on the plaited rope with a lamp of fat in a hollowed stone; the lamp goes small and the dark closes over it, the rope runs out to its last knot and hangs, and after a long while it jerks twice and is hauled up slowly.

events.title: The youth comes up ash-faced and silent
events.body: The youth comes over the lip with his lamp out and his face the colour of ash, and never says, then or in all the years he lives, what was at the bottom; after him no one goes down again.

events.title: The young keeper takes up the turning
events.body: The old keeper of the basins dies and is buried on the slope nearest the water; a young woman who came up as a girl with a father whose ribs were stove in takes up the setting and the turning the next morning, and sets three bones that day.

events.title: A child's broken skull mended by the first basin
events.body: A child fallen from a kiln wall is carried two days to the springs by its mother with the bone above its ear broken; the young keeper lays it by the steam of the first basin, washes the break and binds it loosely, and on the fourth morning it wakes and asks for food.

events.title: Heated stones laid in the third basin in a dry summer
events.body: In a dry summer when the water runs low from the three mouths, the keepers of the basins lay stones heated in a fire into the third basin to bring it back to the warmth the sick need.

events.title: The last stone set by lamplight
events.body: One man, left alone at Làrach an Dùin-fhaire's gate at dusk after the others have gone to other work within the walls, fits the last stones into the gap by a lamp burning down, and presses the last one home with the flat of his hand. Where he went after is not told.

events.title: The rope of the shaft cut up for mooring lines
events.body: After the youth comes up silent, the plaited rope is cut up for mooring lines, and the grown people of the south-east walk wider of the shaft's lip than before.

events.title: The youth will not let a lamp burn low
events.body: The youth who went down the eastern shaft, grown and married at a landing two days south, is known for nothing strange except that he rises in the night to trim or put out any lamp burning low.

events.title: The kerbed way greens over
events.body: With no one going down off the spur, the grass creeps in over the slabs of the kerbed way from its edges, and the kerbs show through the turf like the bones of a thing half buried.

events.title: A woman finds the cistern choked
events.body: A woman of the three rings, going at first light to draw water for her sick father, finds the cistern full of whole cattle, unbutchered, their backs and bent legs breaking the dark water; no one of the rings can say who did it, and no one draws from it again.

events.title: Water carried up the height every morning
events.body: With the cistern of the three rings fouled, every household on the height carries its water up from the valley springs on its own back, a whole morning's labour every morning.

events.title: The first households go down from the rings
events.body: Some households of the three rings tire of the water-carrying before they tire of the height, and go down the track to the lower valleys, saying they go only for the winter.

events.title: Fewer fires burn along Làrach an Dùin wall
events.body: Through a hard winter the coast-people left within the three rings let the farthest fires along the middle wall go dark first, feeding what fuel is left toward those nearest the gate, so that the chain of lights along the rampart burns shorter and thicker each week that passes.

events.title: The last fire in the rings is let go down
events.body: The last of the coast-people still keeping Làrach an Dùin finds every other fire along the wall dark one morning, tends her own alone three days more, then spreads its embers thin across the stone and walks out through the gate and down toward the valleys, carrying nothing from the place she had not carried into it.

events.title: Grass in the threshold of the rings
events.body: Within a few winters of the last fire along the middle wall, grass finds a footing in the gate threshold of the three rings, where the feet of four hundred once kept the stone bare.

events.title: A grandfather of the western landing will not speak of the height
events.body: An old man long settled among shore kin who never went up answers his grandson's question about Làrach an Dùin only with the cold and the wind that found a man through doubled wool, and will say nothing of why he left it or whether he meant, at the time, to come back.

events.title: A household from the rings comes down to Morn
events.body: A household of five comes down from the three rings to the kilns at Morn with nothing but what it can carry, its one ox lost on the scree; the landing takes it in, and the women are set to the kilns, where the younger learns in one morning that a kiln fire must smoke and not flame.

events.title: The southern middens grow faster than living memory
events.body: As more of the coast-people settle at the shore than the shore has ever held, the middens of the southern landing thicken season on season with the ordinary leavings of a people's swelling numbers, and a landing once counted by the dozen comes to be counted by the score.

events.title: The son's wife learns a kiln must not flame
events.body: The keeper of the middle kiln at Morn leads a woman new down from the heights by the wrist to a smouldering kiln and holds her hand over its rack until she understands what three tellings in words had not taught her.

events.title: A girl from the heights sees the sea
events.body: A girl of eight born within the innermost ring is lifted onto a rock above Morn by her grandfather and turned to face the sea, and asks, after a long look, whether it ever stops moving.

events.title: A worked stone kept on a shore shelf
events.body: An old man come down from a height keeps on a shelf at the shore a worked stone no one there has a use for, and it is laid in the stone box with him when his time comes.

events.title: Three men climb to the temple with prising-bars
events.body: Three men of the last kin that still tends the temple climb its steps on a grey autumn morning with bars of seasoned oak shod with bone, the eldest of them a man past sixty who has climbed on the shortest morning every year of his life.

events.title: The altar's top stone is prised free
events.body: Working the better part of the morning, two of the three break out the old clay from the sockets with the points of their bars while the eldest stands with his hands flat on the stone, and a while past noon they lift it whole from the sockets it has held since before anyone could remember.

events.title: The altar stone is carried west out of sight
events.body: Slung between the three in a net of hide rope on the same bars, the altar stone is carried down the platform steps and over the shoulder of the hill to the west; it is never found.

events.title: The temple platform goes untended
events.body: No one of that kin climbs the temple steps on the shortest morning again; grass comes in between the platform's fitted stones, and the easy last step that every child of the valley once found with a bare foot in the dark is lost under turf.

events.title: A cairn built below the empty sockets
events.body: The eldest of the three who prised the altar goes up alone years after and spends most of a day building a small cairn of loose stone below the empty sockets, capped square, and comes down with his hands scraped raw, and does not say what it is for.

events.title: The easy last step lost under turf
events.body: The last step of the temple platform, flush with the moor, which every child of the valley once found with a bare foot in the dark, is lost under turf, and the climb begins now with a stumble.

events.title: Eòghann born to the keeper's hearth
events.body: Eòghann is born the second child of the household that keeps the bag and Poit an Teine at Tobar dhìreach, not first looked to for the keeping while his elder sister lives.

events.title: Eòghann counts the coals into his palm as a child
events.body: Eòghann, free of the keeping as a younger son, counts the three coals into his own small palm long before anyone asks it of him, turning them over for the plain pleasure of a smooth thing in the hand.

events.title: The keeping falls to Eòghann
events.body: Eòghann's sister dies of a fever in her nineteenth year, and the bag of three dark coals and the recital pass to Eòghann on his father's death soon after; he is twenty.

events.title: Eòghann's sister dies and his father is buried
events.body: Eòghann's elder sister dies of a fever in her nineteenth year, and his father is buried beside Leac na Fèithe the same season, so that the keeping comes to Eòghann at twenty.

events.title: Eòghann marries Dearbhail
events.body: Eòghann takes Dearbhail of the lake-shore line, who keeps his fire-pot and his hearth through the long absences his walking keeps him to.

events.title: Gual airgid carried to the home river and two more
events.body: In his first years of keeping Eòghann carries gual airgid to the Abhainn ghorm below Tobar dhìreach, to two rivers besides, and to a mountain tarn, in case the water nearest the hearth had never been fairly asked; none answers him.

events.title: A mountain tarn tried for the silver
events.body: Among the waters Eòghann tries gual airgid against is a mountain tarn that is no river at all but holds, by the telling, water enough to be worth the asking; it does not answer.

events.title: Eòghann keeps the old custom of the shore
events.body: With nothing newly occurring to him, Eòghann carries the three dark coals north to the shore his father once brought him to, to throw them into the sea in the old way, out of a custom kept past most keepers' belief in it.

events.title: The three coals thrown into the sea again for nothing
events.body: Eòghann throws the silver, the untried, and gual bogha-froise into the grey swell off the northern shore in the falling light, and wades in after them to find them as dark and salt-wet as they went in.

events.title: Eòghann walks home through two days of rain
events.body: Eòghann turns south for Tobar dhìreach the morning after the casting, walking two wet days over moor and birch scrub with his mind on nothing beyond the ground in front of him.

events.title: Eòghann kneels and drinks at the crossing
events.body: Thirsty and tired on the last stretch of the road home, Eòghann kneels at the crossing of the Abhainn ghorm below Tobar dhìreach and drinks, and says aloud, to no one, that this water tastes different from the sea water.

events.title: Gual airgid catches under the current
events.body: Eòghann throws the three dark coals into the river at the crossing without weighing the throw, and gual airgid catches beneath the surface, a pale fire standing in the current that the water cannot quench.

events.title: The two dark coals found on a gravel bar
events.body: Gual teine and the rainbow, rolled on past Eòghann by the current in the dark, are found at first light lodged cold against a bar of gravel a stone's throw below the crossing, and carried home in the bag as dark as they went into the water.

events.title: The fifth coal named at the recital
events.body: At the next telling of the Line, Eòghann speaks the new line into the recital: the sea, the height, the earth and a man's own blood have answered, and now the river has taken the fifth, given rather than thrown to it, and the valley names it gual airgid.

events.title: The silver burns on under the crossing
events.body: Gual airgid goes on burning under the current at the shallow crossing below Tobar dhìreach, a low pale light any traveller may kneel at the bank and see on a dark evening.

events.title: Travellers come to see the fire under the water
events.body: Word of the pale fire standing under the current draws travellers to the crossing below Tobar dhìreach in numbers greater than the ford had ever seen, some kneeling to drink the same water Eòghann drank without finding it tastes to them any different.

events.title: Eòghann tells the taste cannot be looked for
events.body: Pressed to say what he tasted in the river, Eòghann owns that he cannot put it into words and holds that a man cannot go looking for that taste and find it sooner than he himself found it, kneeling thirsty.

events.title: Eòghann tries gual teine against flint
events.body: In his later keeping Eòghann strikes gual teine against flint more than once, hoping the snap of a hand the tellers spoke of might be struck rather than fallen into, and gets from it no more than the ordinary spark any stone gives a blade.

events.title: Eòghann dies at his own hearth
events.body: Eòghann dies in his six-and-sixtieth year at Tobar dhìreach, Poit an Teine burning near him, his last words not of the coals but of the crossing, asking whether the water still ran clear and the light still stood under it.

events.title: The bag passes on with two coals still dark
events.body: The leather bag, with gual teine and gual bogha-froise still unanswered, passes from Eòghann's grave to a younger kinsman of the line, as it passed from Cormac's before him.

events.title: Fewer of the coast-people climb to the temple
events.body: In the years before the temple stands empty for good, those of the landings who still climb to Làrach an Teampaill go up fewer at a time and stay a shorter while at the top, as a household goes on setting a place at table for a while after the one who sat in it has stopped coming.

events.title: A woman climbs to the temple with empty hands
events.body: A woman of the landings climbs the temple's steps alone at first light and comes down again at evening with nothing in her hands either time, and no one after her is known to climb to Làrach an Teampaill again.

events.title: Grass takes the temple platform
events.body: With no foot left to keep it short, the grass between the temple platform's fitted stones grows up thick, and the altar's empty sockets are left to fill and empty again with nothing but whatever season sends into them.

events.title: Whole kin-groups come down from the abandoned heights
events.body: Where ones and single families once drifted down from the empty heights to settle at the shore, whole kin-groups now come down together, until the landing at Cwen holds more people at once than any landing has held before.

events.title: A rower teaches the gulls' warning
events.body: Rowers of Slighe-mhara àrsaidh keep a plain word for anyone new to the stretch north of the cape: watch the gulls before you watch the sky, for the birds leave that water before a man in it feels what is coming.

events.title: No new work raised out of sight of salt water
events.body: After the high places are left, the people of the landings raise no new work anywhere out of sight of salt water, and the shore takes back all the labour the heights had drawn away.

events.title: The midden at Cwen outgrows the midden at Dunn
events.body: The midden below the southern landing at Cwen, thickened season on season by the swelling numbers settled there, grows past the midden at Dunn, which had for a lifetime and more been the largest heap of shell and bone the coast could show.

events.title: A landing once counted by the dozen is counted by the score
events.body: Two rowers of the sea-way, meeting off a landing-stone, trade the season's news: more households at Cwen than either can remember from a single year before, and a landing further north near empty of the families that once worked it.

events.title: The sea-way's landing-stones grooved by keels
events.body: Season on season of hauled keels wear clear grooves into the flat landing-stones of Slighe-mhara àrsaidh along the south-east coast, so that a rower of that lane comes to know each stone by its wear as surely as by its place along the shore.

events.title: A father teaches his son the sea-way stone by stone
events.body: A rower of Slighe-mhara àrsaidh carries his son in the bow through a whole season's rowing, naming each landing-stone as it comes until the boy's own eye can find the next one before his father's voice does, the same teaching the lane is given, before and after, to every rower's son.

events.title: Rathnait born to the valleys about the crack
events.body: Rathnait is born the third child of a household two ridges east of Tobar dhìreach, of no line that keeps a fire-pot or counts fathers back to the mason by name, but of the valleys about the crack all the same.

events.title: The valleys' dead laid facing the mountains
events.body: The households of the high valleys lay their dead in the ground on their side with the knees drawn up and the face toward the central mountains, with an uncut stone set on end at the head and no mark on it.

events.title: An elder doubts the new name will last
events.body: At Oidhche an Dealanaich an old woman of the ford hears the households called Clann nan Dè for the first time and will not say the word herself, having watched other names tried at other gatherings in her own long life and none of them outlast the fire that first warmed them into being said.

events.title: An old man of the west gives the name Clann nan Dè
events.body: At the gathering on Oidhche an Dealanaich an old man of the western household answers a stranger's question with a word for the whole of the gathered valleys: Clann nan Dè.

events.title: The name carried to hearths not at the gathering
events.body: The name Clann nan Dè is said the next night of the lightning at hearths that were not at the western gathering, carried to them as a coal is carried from one hearth to a cold one three valleys off.

events.title: Clann nan Dè settles into ordinary use
events.body: By the time Rathnait is old enough to sit among the elders at her own hearth's turn to hold the gathering, the name Clann nan Dè is said across the valleys about the crack as plainly and as unremarked as any older name tied to a single ridge or ford.

events.title: Rathnait dies among the valleys she named
events.body: Rathnait dies at her own household's hearth, having carried the word she first heard tried at a stranger's fire into ordinary use across the whole of the valleys about the crack.
